task: open the cabinet, take out the object, put it on the bench

fridge.note: A cabinet with a hinged door and a handle, standing on the bench. The task is to open it, take out what is inside, and put that on the bench. It is here because every task so far has been about an object that was simply lying there. This one has a mechanism in it, and the door's arc is a constraint the arm has to obey rather than a path it gets to choose.

door.note: Hinged on the far side and opened by pulling the near edge toward the arm, so the door ends up as a wall off to one side and the opening faces the arm. The swing limit is what makes this articulated: the handle may travel along exactly one arc, and any pull not tangent to it is a pull the hinge refuses.

handle.note: A vertical bar on brackets, so a parallel gripper closing along its own x axis can take it from in front. It stands 82 mm off the door because the fingers are 70 mm long: at the 38 mm it started at, the jaws closed with one pad on the handle and the other 9 N deep into the door panel, holding the door SHUT while the arm pulled. A handle has to have room behind it for the hand. The brackets sit at the two ENDS of the bar, not its middle. With one central bracket the jaws closed with one pad on the bar and the other 9 N into the bracket behind it, which is a grip on the door rather than on the handle. Real handles mount at the ends for exactly this reason: the middle has to be free for a hand. The bar is 180 mm long with its brackets 164 mm apart, because the wrist plate is 80 mm tall and sits 47 mm behind the grasp centre -- so whenever the gripper holds the bar, the plate is INSIDE the bracket span. At the original 96 mm spacing that left 8 mm of margin a side, and any misalignment as the door swung jammed the plate between the brackets at 280 N, which no retreat could pull against. A handle has to have room for the whole hand, not just the fingers.
